claims.text: A homogeneous, single-phase Ti-Hf-Zr-Mo-W solid solution with every element at or above 5 at.% can serve as the starting material.
Slow cooling minimizes residual lattice distortions in Ti-Hf-Zr-Mo-W.
Rapid quenching maximizes lattice strain or disorder in Ti-Hf-Zr-Mo-W.
The samples should be compared only after verifying comparable phase purity and compositional homogeneity.
Cooling rate can affect secondary-phase formation in high-entropy alloys, making phase purity a relevant control.
The relevant structural mediator is the degree of local lattice distortion and associated inhomogeneous strain.
Greater quench-induced lattice distortion alters the local phonon spectrum.
Superconductivity in the proposed Ti-Hf-Zr-Mo-W alloy is governed by effective electron-phonon coupling.
The phonon changes produced by greater lattice distortion reduce the effective electron-phonon interaction strength.
Reduced effective electron-phonon coupling lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
Rapidly quenched samples will have a lower Tc than slowly cooled samples.
Slow-cooled samples will exhibit a higher or more robust Tc than rapidly quenched samples.
The proposed mechanism applies only while Ti-Hf-Zr-Mo-W remains single-phase and compositionally homogeneous.
Segregation or secondary-phase formation would confound attribution of Tc changes solely to lattice strain.
X-ray diffraction and phonon spectroscopy can be used to quantify the proposed structural and vibrational mediators, while resistivity and magnetic susceptibility can determine Tc.
Failure of quenching to produce different distortion or phonon spectra, together with no Tc difference, would falsify the mechanism.
